title: Verified Cool-Night Rooms for Heat-Stressed Europe
one_liner: Cheap in-room sensors prove a hotel room stays below about 26C at night, sold as a certificate, a refund guarantee and a machine-readable rating for booking agents.
customer: Hotels, B&Bs and STR operators in Greece, Italy, Spain, Croatia, Portugal and Turkey, with OTAs, agent builders and insurers as secondary buyers.
problem: Summer heat makes 'air-conditioned' meaningless, since old units, weak cooling and poor insulation leave rooms hot at night. Nobody measures indoor night temperature, so complaints turn into refund disputes. Rerouted demand into Turkey and Southern Europe, and a focus on 'value for money', make heat a rising complaint.
solution: Fit a USD 10-15 wireless sensor per room in about 10 minutes. It logs a nightly indoor temperature curve, and we issue a 'Cool Night verified' certificate showing the share of nights below the threshold, with a public verification page and JSON feed for AI agents and metasearch. Hotels also get a dashboard to find and fix problem rooms, and can add a hotel-funded heat refund guarantee.
why_now: Repeated European heatwaves, cheap connected sensors, and AI booking assistants that need structured, verifiable attributes because star ratings and 'AC yes/no' are uninformative. Booking's commoditisation of listings makes measured differentiation valuable to independents.
revenue_model: EUR 6-9 per room per month, a EUR 150 install kit, an annual certification fee, and data licensing to platforms.
non_obvious_insight: Comfort is the one hotel attribute that is physically measurable yet almost never measured. In a world of agent-driven booking, a verified physical attribute becomes a ranking signal.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 hotels in Athens, Crete, Sicily and Puglia using off-the-shelf sensors. Offer a free 30-day 'truth test' and publish an anonymised heat report for press. Convert 10 to paid subscriptions.

title: Forever Guardian: Lifetime Care After Parents Are Gone
one_liner: A prepaid, life-insurance-funded successor-care plan in which a named team becomes the lifelong advocate, money manager and care coordinator for an adult with a disability after the parents are gone.
customer: Parents in their 60s-80s of adult children with intellectual or developmental disabilities (nearly one million US households have adults with I/DD living with an aging caregiver). Referred by special-needs planning attorneys and financial planners.
problem: Parents dread 'who will look after them when we're gone.' Siblings are often unavailable, state Medicaid waiver waitlists are long, pooled special-needs trusts manage money but rarely relationships, and no single accountable person exists for decades. The current autism generation is about to become adults, and the adult cohort will surge.
solution: A tiered plan. (1) While parents are alive: a named care manager, annual home visit, a living 'letter of intent' binder (routines, medications, preferences), and monthly check-in calls, so the person already knows the successor. (2) At transition: the team acts as advocate or guardian-of-record where allowed, coordinates services, audits group-home quality, and works with a partner trust company holding a pooled special-needs trust. (3) Funded by a paid-up second-to-die life policy or an upfront fee plus a monthly retainer.
why_now: Peak-65 parents are hitting the age where the successor question is urgent, Medicaid home- and community-based services are under financial pressure, and adults with I/DD are living longer than any prior generation. It is a large, emotionally urgent market with no scaled, for-profit successor-care provider.
revenue_model: Upfront enrollment ($5-15k or insurance-funded), a monthly care-management retainer ($100-200), trust administration fees through the partner, and insurance commissions.
non_obvious_insight: The real product is a relationship that starts before the parents die. The annual home visit is both the moat and the sales funnel: by the time a parent passes, the guardian is already someone the adult knows and trusts. It converts a frightening legal product into a service with visible value every month while the parents are still alive to judge it.
first_30_days: Partner with three special-needs planning attorneys and one trust company. Sign 15 families to a $1,500 'Shadow Year' (assessment, letter-of-intent binder, quarterly visits, monthly calls). Hire one care manager and validate the guardianship, trust and licensing requirements for a single state before promising the full lifetime plan.

title: Narrow Networks and Reference Pricing for Pet Insurers
one_liner: Pet insurers reimburse whatever clinics invoice while losing about 10 points a year to price/mix inflation; build the pet-insurance 'PPO' from affordable-care clinics whose invoices run about 44% lower.
customer: Mid-size pet insurers and MGAs (payers), affordable-care and team-based independent clinics (network), and insured owners steered by a lower deductible or higher reimbursement in-network.
problem: 2025 premiums grew about 19.7% against 9% growth in insured animals, and insurers do not contract with clinics, so they have no lever on price. Owners face renewal shock. Corporate chains (Mars about 2,100 clinics; GoodVets going from 75 to 116) are bound to margin targets and are unlikely to cut price.
solution: Contract a metro-by-metro network of independent affordable-care clinics with agreed fee schedules, standardized service coding and direct pay. The insurer offers an in-network tier (for example, 90% reimbursement with no deductible on routine lines). We provide claims routing, spectrum-of-care quality guardrails, and network-savings reporting. Start with one metro.
why_now: The premium/enrollment gap is now visible in trade press, roll-ups are accelerating, and the affordable-care model is documented at $130 vs $233 average invoices. Model-law adoption is pushing insurers toward transparency and cost containment.
revenue_model: Shared savings (20-30% of verified savings vs a market baseline) or 3-5% administration fee on network claims. Clinics pay nothing.
non_obvious_insight: 'Reimburse at any vet' is sold as a feature, but in human health the equivalent indemnity design gave way to networks once cost trend outran wages. Steering is the only demand-side lever pet insurance has not pulled, and the low-priced independent tier is spare capacity waiting for volume.
first_30_days: Identify 15-20 team-based or low-cost independents in one metro. Get an NDA with one small insurer or MGA and pull 200 claims. Reprice them against the network fee schedule to show projected savings (target 15% or more). Propose a 6-month shared-savings pilot on an existing product tier.

title: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge Eligibility and Prior-Auth Navigator
one_liner: A 2-minute eligibility check and clinician-ready prior-auth packet for the $50/month Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, sold to caregivers, independent pharmacies and primary-care offices before the window closes in December 2027.
customer: Two payers. (a) Gen X adult children (45-58, household income often above $100K) who manage a Medicare-age parent's medications and pay $29 per packet. (b) Independent pharmacies and small primary-care practices that pay $79/month to stop fielding the same eligibility and prior-auth questions by phone.
problem: Medicare started an 18-month GLP-1 Bridge on July 1, 2026. It costs $50/month for Wegovy, Zepbound or Foundayo, but eligibility is a maze. It needs a BMI of 35 or more, or BMI 30+ with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, uncontrolled hypertension or stage 3a+ kidney disease, or BMI 27+ with pre-diabetes, prior heart attack or stroke, or symptomatic peripheral artery disease. Type 2 diabetes, sleep apnea and MASH disqualify you. So does having filled any GLP-1 under Part D in 2026. Prior authorization is required. Roughly 3.8M Part D enrollees qualify and about 5.9M are locked out, so sicker patients are routed to Part D copays of $200-600+ a month. One 68-year-old retired professor with BMI 42, a quadruple bypass and sleep apnea told KFF Health News: 'I'm obese, morbidly obese, BMI 42... And yet I can't get it.'
solution: A plain-language quiz built from the published Bridge criteria. It flags the traps, such as a 2026 Part D GLP-1 fill or a sleep apnea diagnosis. It outputs one of three routes: Bridge, Part D with an expected copay, or a manufacturer cash price (TrumpRx lists $149-$299/month). It then generates a prior-authorization documentation checklist and cover letter for the prescriber (BMI evidence, comorbidity codes, exclusion attestation). Pharmacies and practices get a white-label link and a shared queue of who is waiting on what. It stays plan-neutral: no plan enrollment and no commissions from carriers, which keeps it outside Medicare marketing rules (confirm with counsel).
why_now: The Bridge began July 1, 2026 and ends December 2027, so the demand window is 15 months and open enrollment starts October 15, about 3 weeks from now. CMS is also ending the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026. That subsidy had cut average premiums by $26 in 2025 and $16 in 2026, and about 24.9M people are in stand-alone drug plans that may face bigger 2027 increases. Oral options (Wegovy pill approved December 2025, Foundayo approved April 2026) widen the eligible pool. Nobody has built a workflow product for a program this new and this temporary.
revenue_model: $29 one-time per beneficiary packet (caregiver-paid). $79/month per independent pharmacy or clinic for white-label link, queue and templates. Optional $15 per completed PA-submission assist. Sunset risk is real, so design the engine to carry over to whatever CMS replaces the Bridge with (KFF flags a coming BALANCE model).
non_obvious_insight: The eligibility rules create a paradox where the sicker you are, the more you pay. Sleep apnea or diabetes disqualifies patients from the $50 Bridge and pushes them into $200-600+ Part D copays, which can exceed manufacturer cash prices ($199 Wegovy pen, $299 Zepbound on TrumpRx). That gap creates demand for a neutral router rather than another telehealth prescriber. Evidence: KFF's Bridge criteria, cost and start/end dates https://www.kff.org/medicare/nearly-four-million-medicare-beneficiaries-met-the-eligibility-criteria-in-2023-for-the-medicare-glp-1-bridge/ ; the excluded-patient quote, 5.9M figure and Part D copay range https://kffhealthnews.org/aging/medicare-glp1-bridge-weight-loss-drugs-coverage-exceptions-cost-access/ ; premium-subsidy end and 24.9M stand-alone enrollees https://www.kff.org/quick-insights/cmss-decision-to-end-temporary-subsidies-to-medicares-stand-alone-drug-plans-could-mean-larger-premium-increases-for-some-beneficiaries-next-year/ ; cash prices https://trumprx.gov/ . To verify: whether Medicare beneficiaries can actually use cash-price channels, and how those purchases interact with Part D cap accounting. One fetched source (Wikipedia) implies TrumpRx has Medicare-specific pricing, which conflicts with the site's consumer prices.
first_30_days: Week 1: turn the KFF criteria into a quiz and publish 'Do I qualify for the $50 Medicare GLP-1 Bridge?' pages timed to the October 15 open-enrollment spike. Week 2: post in Medicare and caregiver communities and pitch 10 independent pharmacies (NCPA-style networks) on a free white-label link. Week 3: get one primary-care practice to review the PA cover-letter template for clinical accuracy. Week 4: charge $29 for the packet. Target 100 paid packets and 5 pharmacies on $79/month. Keep it free of plan recommendations until compliance is reviewed.

title: Independent Audits for Per-Outcome Agent Invoices
one_liner: The DoubleVerify of AI agents: sample and verify the resolutions, meetings and approvals you were billed for, then claim credits for the fakes.
customer: Finance, procurement and support-ops leaders at companies paying $50k-$5M a year to outcome-priced agent vendors (support resolutions, AP processing, claims, scheduling).
problem: Vendors have moved from seats to outcomes. Reportedly, Zendesk narrowed billing to LLM-verified 'resolutions' at about $1.20-$1.50 each and HubSpot's customer agent charges about $0.50 per resolved conversation. The vendor defines and grades its own outcome, and buyers cannot tell a real resolution from a customer who gave up. Step two of falling token prices is vendors with an incentive to over-count outcomes.
solution: A read-only connector to the buyer's helpdesk, CRM or ERP that re-derives outcomes independently from reopen rates, repeat contacts in 7-14 days, silent abandonment, escalation to humans and sentiment. Sample about 300 outcomes a month for blind human plus LLM review. Deliver a monthly invoice integrity report with the false-outcome rate and a credit-claim packet aligned to the contract's dispute window.
why_now: Outcome pricing became mainstream in 2026, and Deloitte published guidance in June 2026 on accounting for it, which signals CFO attention. Buyers paying per outcome have no independent measurement.
revenue_model: 10-20% of credits recovered plus a $2-6k/month subscription. The buy side pays first to avoid conflict, and vendors may later pay for an audited badge.
non_obvious_insight: Ad tech showed that when sellers measure their own outcomes, a third-party verifier becomes a category (DoubleVerify, IAS). Agent outcome pricing recreates that conflict with almost no independent measurement, and the earliest data is anonymous benchmarks of false-resolution rates.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 companies using Fin, Zendesk or HubSpot agents through support-ops communities. Run a free or contingency retrospective audit of 3 months of invoices and publish anonymized false-resolution rates to seed demand.

title: Shelved-Game Rescue Exchange
one_liner: A broker that packages cancelled and orphaned game prototypes and licenses them to laid-off veteran teams on revenue-share terms, with reversion rights if the game stalls.
customer: Publishers, closing studios and insolvency administrators holding unreleased builds (they get a recovery instead of a write-off). The paying counterparties are veteran-led small teams and the funders behind them.
problem: Ubisoft cancelled six games in Jan 2026 and cut headcount from 18,666 to 16,590. EA's owners closed a $55B LBO with $20B of debt and a stated plan to cut costs with AI. Cancelled projects sit unused with teams disbanded, while laid-off veterans have skills but no IP or prototype budget.
solution: Build a 'prototype data room' per project: build, design docs, and a third-party licence and music clearance audit. Add a standard rescue licence (revenue share, milestone reversion, credit terms) and a registry of veteran team leads. Match the two, and offer milestone-funded finishing through a small fund or partner investors. Start with insolvent and small publishers, which move faster than Ubisoft or EA legal.
why_now: The 2023-26 layoff wave left an unusually deep bench of finished-quality talent. The EA LBO and Ubisoft restructuring guarantee more shelved work. Steam distribution and Epic's 0% fee on the first $1M make a 10-20 person finish economically viable.
revenue_model: 10-15% of the licensee's revenue share, or a success fee at signing ($10-50k), plus a data-room packaging fee paid by the rights holder.
non_obvious_insight: A shelved game's cost to its owner is legal and opportunity overhead, not the code. A zero-upfront licence with reversion beats a write-down and avoids a public fire sale. Insiders assume cancelled means bad, but many projects die for portfolio or budget-cycle reasons, not quality.
first_30_days: Publish a public 'orphaned prototypes wanted' page. Call 20 insolvency administrators and mid-size publishers found through recent studio-closure announcements with a one-page offer. Have a games lawyer draft the rescue licence. Recruit 10 veteran-led teams from layoff communities on Discord and LinkedIn. Aim for one signed rescue by day 60.

title: Hybrid-Race-in-a-Box Rentals for Gyms
one_liner: Rentable station kits, timing, waivers, insurance and sanitation protocols so any gym can run a Hyrox-style event for members.
customer: Independent gyms and CrossFit-style boxes (pay $2.5-4k per event); secondary: run-club organizers and corporate wellness days.
problem: Chain: Hyrox's global boom (events selling out, new markets such as Kuala Lumpur in December 2026) makes members demand local competitions, but official events are capacity-limited and licensed; local copycats need eight stations of gear, timing, heat management and a medical plan; and the Beijing incident (an athlete kept racing after soiling herself on shared equipment, prompting an apology and new biohazard rules) shows sanitation is a brand-level risk. Nobody sells a standardized, insured kit.
solution: A trailerized 8-station kit with standard loading specs, chip or QR bib timing through a phone app, wipe-down protocol cards and biohazard kit, medical response plan, waiver and event-insurance pack, and a results page. The gym sells tickets; we take rental plus a per-athlete fee.
why_now: Hybrid racing went mainstream in 2025-26, hygiene and safety incidents have made organizers seek documented protocols, and used sleds and ergs are cheap.
revenue_model: $2.5-4k per event rental plus about $5 per athlete for timing and insurance; sell kits to multi-gym operators at $18-30k.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not the format but the logistics and liability packaging for local operators; for a gym the payoff is member retention and lead generation from ticket buyers who are not yet members.
first_30_days: Buy $12-15k of used sleds, ballast and ergs, run a first event with a partner gym to document cost per athlete, offer three other gyms discounted rentals, and build a small QR-bib timing page.

title: Dark-Core Muscle Clinics in Converting Offices
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare/GLP-1/longevity/consumer health x Real estate (office-to-resi, vacancy, property mgmt, affordability)
one_liner: A plug-in metabolic and muscle clinic sized for the windowless middle of deep office floor plates that developers cannot turn into apartments, so dead space earns rent and GLP-1 users get an in-building place to keep their muscle.
customer: Office-to-residential developers and their lenders with deep-floorplate buildings (they gain a rent line on unusable area). Demand side: GLP-1 users who live or work in the building, plus employers that dropped GLP-1 coverage (employer coverage fell from 72% to 60% in 2026) and want a capped-cost program.
problem: Conversions only pencil when every bedroom can have a window, so deep floor plates lose a large share of each floor to unrentable middle or need expensive light wells. Meanwhile only about a third of non-diabetic GLP-1 patients persist at 1 year, stoppers regain weight roughly 4x faster than behavioral losers, and muscle loss is unmanaged. Nobody is paid to run a supervised strength-and-nutrition protocol close to where patients live and work.
solution: A standardized 3,000-6,000 sf module: body-composition scan, 6-8 supervised strength stations, dietitian rooms, lab draw, telehealth booths and pill-pickup lockers, run by a prescriber-agnostic clinical group so members can bring a Wegovy or Foundayo script from anywhere. Ambulatory clinics are Group B occupancy like offices, so no change of use is needed. Developers get a 'core-fill' master lease (low $/sf plus a slice of membership revenue) that improves conversion math and gives lenders a credit-tested income line. Members pay about $99/mo. Employers pay a capped per-employee fee.
why_now: The Wegovy pill (Jan 2026) and Lilly's Foundayo (Apr 2026) at about $149/mo turned GLP-1s into a mass cash-pay product, so millions of stop-and-restart cycles are coming. Employers are dropping coverage. Office vacancy is 17.8% with $289B of office loans maturing by 2028 and CMBS delinquency at 13.2%, so owners will trade rent for feasibility. Neko Health's $700M raise for a NYC launch shows urban demand for preventive scanning, yet nobody runs the muscle-and-adherence loop after the scan.
revenue_model: Memberships at $79-149/mo; per-member fees from employers and Medicare Advantage plans; body-comp and lab add-ons; a low-rent master lease with revenue share to the landlord.
non_obvious_insight: The thing that kills conversions (no daylight) is the one thing a clinic does not need. Because clinics share office occupancy class, the space is code-legal without a change of use. A clinic inside the building where hundreds of residents and lunch-hour office workers already are may be the highest-adherence location possible for a persistence problem.
first_30_days: Lease one vacant interior suite in a half-empty Class B office at near-zero rent with landlord-funded build-out. Open a 10-week 'GLP-1 muscle lab' with one exercise physiologist, a $10-15K body-composition scanner and a contracted dietitian. Sell 40-60 memberships to workers in the building and 2-3 local employers that dropped coverage. Take the adherence data to conversion developers with deep-plate buildings and sign 1-2 letters of intent.

title: Shared Emergency Desk for Autonomous Fleets
one_liner: A neutral 24/7 first-responder interface (hotline, dispatch API, geofence directives) that small AV, robot-truck and delivery-robot operators rent instead of building.
customer: Newer and second-tier AV operators (autonomous trucking, shuttles, delivery pods, robotaxi entrants), and city and county 911 dispatch centers on the public-facing side.
problem: Regulators are asking for a human phone number, not more autonomy. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on July 8, 2026, and California's AV enforcement rules take effect in 2026 (as I understand them). Waymo alone runs about 70 remote agents per shift from two centers in the Philippines, which small operators cannot copy.
solution: A US-staffed desk trained on fire and police protocols. It offers standardized emergency-response guides, one API through which dispatch centers can stop, unlock or reroute any subscribing fleet, compliance logs, and drills for first responders.
why_now: Driverless trucking is commercial (Aurora about 200 trucks, Gatik 85k driverless orders, Einride listed), new AV entrants are launching, and states are writing rules. Compliance deadlines land in 2026.
revenue_model: $500-2,000 per vehicle per year or an $8-25k monthly fleet retainer, plus training contracts with cities.
non_obvious_insight: A commodity BPO with liability attached scales with vehicle count, and neutrality is a feature because cities prefer one interface for all fleets. Large operators build their own desks, so the long tail of new entrants is the market.
first_30_days: Interview 10 safety and compliance leads at autonomous trucking and delivery-robot companies. Build a minimal hotline plus web console for a single pilot, co-design the protocol with 2 city or county dispatch centers, and sign 2 paid pilots at about $5k a month.

title: Failed-Part Bounty for Insurance Subrogation
one_liner: Pay plumbers a bounty to bag, photograph and chain-of-custody the pipe, supply line or fitting that failed, then sell the evidence and a brand-level failure database to insurers' subrogation units and manufacturers.
customer: Subrogation departments and subro vendors at regional and mutual homeowners insurers (the ones too small to send a forensic engineer to a $9k supply-line loss). Second buyers: plumbing manufacturers, distributors and private-label buyers who license the failure data.
problem: Water damage is among the top two homeowner claim categories. Product-defect subrogation (a supply line, PEX fitting, toilet connector, ice-maker line or water heater that failed early) only works if someone kept the failed part. The plumber is on scene 1 to 3 days before the adjuster, cuts the failed piece out, and tosses it in the truck-bed scrap bin. When the adjuster arrives the evidence is gone, the insurer eats the loss, and the manufacturer's lawyers cite spoliation. Insurers only hire the $2,000 forensic engineer on the big losses, so the routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. Meanwhile every plumber knows which brands are failing (certain plastic-nut braided lines, certain fill valves, certain fitting lots) but nobody aggregates it.
solution: A 90-second protocol and kit. Tamper-evident bag with a QR label, a phone flow (photo of the part in place, photo after removal, the manufacturer stamp or date code, homeowner e-signature by text, and the claim number if one exists). A weekly courier pickup from the shop and a climate-controlled evidence locker. Optional one-page factual cause-of-loss statement drawn from the same photos (sudden burst versus long-term seepage, which is exactly the 'gradual leak' exclusion that decides whether homeowners get paid). Every part is logged by brand, model, date code and failure mode, which builds a Backblaze-style public failure-rate report by product line. Insurers get the part plus a ready evidence package. The shop gets a bounty and a small line item on the invoice.
why_now: Water-loss severity has risen sharply and carriers are under pressure on homeowners loss ratios, so they are hunting for recovery dollars. Copper and steel tariffs plus the shift to PEX and imported fittings have flooded the market with cheaper components of unknown quality. Photo and OCR tooling now makes a cheap, standardized evidence workflow possible, and the subrogation trade press is openly saying evidence preservation is the make-or-break step.
revenue_model: Insurer or subro vendor pays $75-150 per part with a documented chain of custody, of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech. Plus a 3-8% success share on any recovery that follows. Plus annual data licenses ($15-60k) to manufacturers, distributors and big-box private-label buyers, and per-report fees for expert-witness-ready packages.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence that decides tens of millions in recoveries is currently destroyed daily by the only people who touch it first, and the reason is not malice. Nobody pays a tech to spend 4 minutes and a bag on a piece of scrap. The plumber, not the adjuster, is the true first-notice-of-loss for the product itself. The bounty is a price signal, and the dataset that falls out is one nobody else can buy.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and the owner Facebook and peer groups with a flat $50 per bag and a free kit. Design the label and the phone flow in a form tool. Collect the first 50 parts with photos. Take the first 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subrogation vendor and ask them which they would have pursued. Sell a paid pilot for 100 parts on the strength of their answers.

title: Plaintiff-Evidence Pipeline for Kids-Tech Litigation
one_liner: Software and services that automate platform data requests, device-usage exports and chat-log preservation into court-ready per-plaintiff timelines for firms litigating social media and AI-chatbot harms to minors.
customer: Plaintiff-side mass-tort firms and litigation funders with hundreds or thousands of minor-plaintiff clients (the social media adolescent-addiction docket, the AI-chatbot wrongful-death wave). Also expert-witness firms.
problem: Raine v. OpenAI (Aug 2025) opened a wave of suits and the FTC's Sept 2025 6(b) orders raised the stakes. Each plaintiff needs account data from 5-10 platforms, screen-time records and chat exports. Families are non-technical, formats are inconsistent and firms rely on paralegals and spreadsheets.
solution: A client-facing mobile intake that guides each family through data-export requests (Google Takeout, Meta, TikTok, Snap, ChatGPT and Character.AI exports, Screen Time screenshots via OCR). It adds chain-of-custody hashing, normalizes everything into timelines (late-night usage, DM volume, content categories), redacts third-party minors and outputs expert-ready exhibits.
why_now: Trials and settlements in 2026 raise the value of well-documented plaintiffs. The volume of AI-chatbot and social-media suits (including Pennsylvania v. Character.AI, May 2026) is growing faster than firms' ops capacity.
revenue_model: $150-600 per plaintiff processed, or a $2-10k monthly per-firm subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Mass torts are won on aggregate evidence and speed, and the bottleneck is unglamorous plaintiff-level data collection. A picks-and-shovels vendor gets paid whichever side wins.
first_30_days: Contact 10 boutique mass-tort firms via legal-ops networks. Build a Takeout and Meta-export parser prototype. Charge $250 per plaintiff for a pilot batch of 40. Retain a litigation-support consultant for chain-of-custody rules. Work only through counsel, never soliciting families.

title: Contingency Appeals for Denied Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Insurers rely on paperwork friction to keep denials uncontested; LLMs that assemble records and policy language make appeals cheap enough to work for a success fee.
customer: Pet owners with denied or reduced claims of roughly $1,500-$15,000 (pre-existing, bilateral, hereditary or 'curable' exclusion disputes), reached through owner communities and vet front desks.
problem: Premiums rose about 19.7% in 2025 while insured animals grew 9%, so owners are angry and paying more for coverage that may not pay. An appeal requires pulling every prior clinic's records, reading policy definitions and getting a vet statement. Most owners give up.
solution: Owner uploads the denial letter and policy. We automate records requests to past clinics, read records against the policy's definitions and the state's pet-insurance rules, draft the appeal with a contracted DVM's signed medical statement, file it, and escalate to the state insurance department if needed. Fee is 15-25% of recovered dollars, nothing upfront.
why_now: As of early 2026, 28 states had adopted or introduced versions of the NAIC Pet Insurance Model Act, which creates disclosure and pre-existing-condition hooks and formal complaint routes. LLMs can now read messy multi-clinic records cheaply. Premium hikes are driving search intent and anger.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 15-25% of recovered claims. Second product: anonymized denial-pattern intelligence sold to regulators, clinics and insurers who want fewer disputes.
non_obvious_insight: Denial rates are sustained by the cost of contesting, not by the merits. That cost was human labor. Once evidence assembly is near-free, the spread between 'denied' and 'overturned when documented' becomes a business, and it produces the best dataset on how insurers actually deny.
first_30_days: Post 'no win, no fee appeals' in pet-owner communities and take 30 cases. Contract one vet to sign statements at $75-150 each. Track overturn rate; kill criterion is under 20%. Check state public-adjuster and unauthorized-practice rules before charging a contingency fee.

title: Rate-Leak Evidence Packs for Independent Hotels
one_liner: Mystery-shopping plus payout reconciliation that proves when OTA and reseller channels sold below the rate a hotel loaded, packaged as evidence for claims and regulator complaints.
customer: Independent hotels of 20-200 rooms in the EU, UK and US that rely on OTA merchant-model bookings, and hotel associations. The second buyer is a law firm or litigation funder that needs evidence to build a case.
problem: 51% of European hotels say OTAs sell below their loaded rate (up from 40% two years ago), Booking.com handles 66.1% of OTA bookings at surveyed hotels, and 26% of hotels do not know whether rates are passed on. A hotel loads $200, the guest sees $180, and the hotel is paid after checkout. Markups by Agoda, Citi, AA and Southwest loyalty portals are invisible to rate-shopping tools. The only party able to audit the markup is the one being audited.
solution: A panel of real-guest shoppers and reseller-portal quotes covers the hotel's next 90 dates. The results are reconciled against the hotel's folios and payout statements into a 'leak ledger' (date, channel, price shown vs loaded, payout). Timestamped, tamper-evident captures go into a monthly report and an evidence pack the hotel can hand to counsel, an association, a regulator (the EU DMA parity ban) or a claims funder.
why_now: The DMA (Booking designated a gatekeeper in 2024) bans parity clauses, so hotels have new legal options but no proof. The merchant model keeps growing. Fuel and energy shocks (Hormuz, March 2026) and a K-shaped market squeeze lower-tier independents, so recoveries matter.
revenue_model: About EUR 149 per property per month, plus a 20% contingent share of any recovery through a partner law firm or funder. Anonymized leak indices are sold to associations.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence does not exist until someone captures it in real time, and it is perishable because prices change hourly. The firm holding a year of timestamped leaks holds the case file, and OTA self-reporting can never be independent.
first_30_days: Partner with one regional hotel association (Spain, Italy or Croatia). Run a manual 30-date shop of Booking, Expedia, Agoda and two loyalty portals for 20 hotels, and deliver a one-page 'leak map'. Sell a one-off audit at EUR 300, convert 3-5 hotels to the subscription, and take the pack to one litigation funder as proof of concept.

title: Vet-Prescribed Walks for Post-Surgery and Senior Dogs
one_liner: Certify dog walkers to deliver vet-written controlled-walking protocols after cruciate and spinal surgery, and to send structured mobility reports back to the clinic.
customer: Owners of dogs recovering from orthopedic or spinal surgery (TPLO, luxating patella, IVDD) and owners of senior arthritic dogs. Referral partners are surgical and rehab vet practices, who get reports at no charge.
problem: Discharge sheets say things like '5-minute leash walks four times a day, add 5 minutes a week,' and working owners cannot do it. Dogs get over-exercised or under-exercised and some re-tear the repair, which is a $4k to $6k mistake. Most walkers are afraid of the liability, and most vets don't trust an unspecified walker to follow a protocol. Meanwhile arthritic seniors decline slowly and owners miss it, while the walker sees the hesitation at stairs and the shorter walks first.
solution: A short walker certification (protocol cards written with two partner rehab vets, sling and non-slip handling, escalation rules). Visits are timed, leash-controlled, and followed by a structured report covering minutes walked, a 0 to 4 gait score, stiffness on rising, toileting, and a 15-second weight-bearing video. The report goes to the owner and the clinic ahead of the 2, 6, and 8 week rechecks. Red flags (swelling, heat, toe-touching) trigger a same-day call. A senior SKU gives a monthly mobility check with a gait video and pain questionnaire, so owner and vet can see whether joint meds or the newer arthritis injectables are actually working.
why_now: Vets are short-staffed and cannot run rehab follow-ups themselves. Pet insurance adoption keeps growing, so owners protecting a multi-thousand-dollar surgery will pay for compliance. The newer arthritis injectables raised the need for objective at-home response tracking, and safety debates around them make vets want data. Return-to-office pushes more owners out of the house all day right when recoveries need multiple short visits.
revenue_model: Post-op bundle of roughly $900 to $1,800 over 6 to 8 weeks (short visits at $30 to $45), with the walker keeping about 70 percent. Walker certification fee of roughly $250 to $300. Senior monitoring subscription at about $39 a month. No referral kickbacks to vets, so it stays clean; clinics get the free reports and fewer failed recoveries.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable clients in this business are not the healthy dogs on the schedule, they are post-op and declining dogs, because the protocol needs several short, geographically tight visits a day and the owner is desperate. The gap is trust, not supply: a protocol and a report format turn 'a walker' into a rehab extender that vets will refer to.
first_30_days: Sit down with the techs at two local surgical or rehab practices and write a one-page walking progression with them. Get yourself and three walkers through a dry run. Offer the first 10 post-op dogs a reduced bundle in exchange for report feedback, using a simple form that generates a PDF. Ask each clinic to slip a card into TPLO discharge packets and track how many convert.

title: Real-Brine Library and DLE Benchmark Lab
one_liner: A neutral bank of characterised real brines, matrix-matched reference materials and public bake-offs of direct lithium extraction vendors, so nobody has to run a $3M private pilot to compare technologies.
customer: Three payers. First, brine developers (Smackover, Salton Sea geothermal, Argentine and Chilean salars, Utah and Nevada, Canadian oilfield brines) buying screening reports of $15-40k. Second, DLE vendors paying $30-80k per benchmark round for credible independent data. Third, commercial labs paying $2-3k per year for proficiency testing and buying CRMs.
problem: DLE vendors demonstrate on synthetic or 'friendly' brines. Real brines differ in Mg, Ca, Fe, Mn, silica, organics, H2S and temperature. Sorbent life, water balance and reagent cost only show up after hundreds of cycles, so every developer runs its own bespoke pilot ($1-5M, 12-18 months), and claims cannot be compared. On top of that, high-TDS brines (200-400 g/L) are notoriously hard to assay. Different labs disagree by 5-15% because of matrix effects, so 'recovery' computed from assay is shaky. Sealed drums of characterised brine from finished pilots sit unused in every developer's yard.
solution: Collect 12-20 characterised brines, anonymised if the owner wishes, stabilised in sealed drums. Run standardised bench protocols with vendors (50-100 sorption and desorption cycles, membrane or solvent equivalents) and publish scorecards on Li recovery, Mg and Ca rejection, water use, reagent cost per tonne LCE and degradation curve. Sell matrix-matched brine CRMs and inter-laboratory proficiency rounds to labs, and publish a certified-lab list. Developers buy cheap 'technology screening' reports that shortlist vendors before committing to a pilot. Lenders' independent engineers cite the benchmark.
why_now: After the 2023-25 lithium price collapse, investors will only fund bankable, independently verified technology. A wave of DLE technology-selection decisions is happening now in the Smackover, Argentina (RIGI-backed projects), Chile and geothermal brines. The vendor field is crowded and undifferentiated, so vendors will pay for third-party proof.
revenue_model: Vendor benchmark fees ($30-80k per brine set), developer report subscriptions ($15-40k per year), CRM sales, and proficiency-test scheme fees ($2-3k per lab per year), plus certification.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone thinks DLE is a chemistry problem. In practice it is a brine-specific reliability and data-credibility problem, and no one has standard reference brines, so every claim is unfalsifiable. The killers are minor components (silica, organics, Fe and Mn oxidation) that wreck sorbents after 200 cycles, which a fast pilot on an easy brine never shows. The insider knows that the leftover barrel is the asset.
first_30_days: Ask five friendly developers and labs for 20 L of retained brine (leftover after pilots). Characterise each with two labs. Invite three DLE vendors to co-fund a bake-off on one shared brine. Sell an inter-laboratory round to 6 labs at $2k each (about $12k in the first month) and pre-sell a $10k screening report to 3 developers. Publish the interlab bias chart as the marketing piece.

title: Defense Magnet and Tungsten Provenance Dossiers
one_liner: A shared investigator that produces audit-ready provenance files on magnets and tungsten parts for the sub-tier suppliers who cannot get answers from their distributors.
customer: Small and mid-size defense sub-tier suppliers (motors, actuators, sensors, drones, speakers) that buy NdFeB, SmCo magnets or tungsten parts through distributors.
problem: DFARS magnet and tungsten sourcing restrictions extend to upstream mining and refining stages from January 2027. Small suppliers cannot compel Chinese-linked distributors or sinterers to disclose provenance, and primes will demand attestations.
solution: A dossier per part family: supplier questionnaires, document and mill-cert review, distributor-to-sinterer trace-back, and optional lab fingerprinting (trace-element and isotopic) via partner labs. It includes an attestation vault ready for prime audits and an approved-source list of non-covered and recycled suppliers.
why_now: The January 2027 DFARS deadline is about three months away as of late September 2026. Government equity deals (MP, Lithium Americas) and the BIS scrap rule show that provenance is now a national-security control.
revenue_model: $4-15K per part family, $1-3K monthly subscription for upkeep and alerts, and lab-test pass-through with margin.
non_obvious_insight: This is a paperwork problem too small for any customer to solve alone. A shared investigator with a growing fingerprint library amortizes the cost across dozens of clients and gets cheaper as it scales.
first_30_days: Build a free 'does this part need proof?' checker. Pull sub-tier contractors from public procurement records and reach out to 100 firms with the January deadline. Line up a partner lab for fingerprinting. Close 5 paid dossiers.

title: Fixed-Price MDR Clinical Evaluation Reports via ASReview
one_liner: A tech-enabled service that uses the open-source ASReview active-learning screener plus medical writers to deliver audit-ready literature-based Clinical Evaluation Reports at a fraction of consultant prices.
customer: EU MDR device makers with 5-50 staff: digital-health and software-as-a-medical-device startups, legacy Class I/IIa/IIb device makers, and regulatory consultants who need white-label capacity.
problem: MDR requires a Clinical Evaluation Report built on a systematic literature review with appraisal, state-of-the-art analysis and ongoing updates. Consultants charge roughly EUR 10-40k for a literature-based CER. Small firms delay certification or withdraw legacy products because of clinical-evaluation cost.
solution: Run the search protocol in PubMed and other open sources, ClinicalTrials.gov and vigilance databases. Screen with ASReview LAB (validated in Nature Machine Intelligence) with the full screening log retained. A medical writer and a clinical expert appraise and sign off. Deliver the CER plus a PRISMA-style flow diagram and search-string appendix, then sell a quarterly 'living' update for post-market clinical follow-up.
why_now: Legacy-device MDR transition deadlines fall in 2027-2028 and notified-body capacity is tight. Half of medtechs report expecting to spend 5% or more of revenue on MDR. ASReview is mature and widely used in academia, but no one packages it for regulatory work.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of EUR 4-9k per literature-based CER on low-risk devices. Recurring literature-update subscriptions of EUR 1.2-3k per year. Wholesale white-label pricing for consultancies.
non_obvious_insight: Notified bodies rarely reject a CER because the science is thin. They reject it because the methodology is undocumented: search protocol, appraisal criteria, equivalence reasoning. ASReview's transparent, reproducible logging is the compliance artifact, so sell reproducibility rather than speed.
first_30_days: Recruit two freelance medical writers and one clinician-reviewer. Publish three sample CER sections for a public device category as proof. Post in regulatory-affairs communities (RAPS chapters, MDR LinkedIn groups). Sell the first five CERs at a design-partner price and use the audit trail from each as the case study.

title: Result-Loop Desk for Scan and Lab Startups
one_liner: An outsourced nurse-and-radiologist desk that closes the loop on abnormal results from full-body scans, MCED tests and mega-panels.
customer: Mid-tier consumer diagnostics operators without downstream care: full-body MRI resellers, regional imaging centers, longevity clinics, mega-panel labs and employer executive-health programs.
problem: A review of 12 studies found 95% of asymptomatic people had at least one abnormal whole-body MRI finding and 91% of those were not clinically relevant (15-30% false-positive rate). Primary-care waits average ~31 days, so patients arrive at their PCP with printouts. Adoption is accelerating (Neko $700M for a NYC launch, Function 1M+ members), and Lp(a) testing hit a wall when Lp(a)HORIZON failed on Sep 4, 2026, leaving many flagged people without a next step.
solution: Triage each flagged result (ignore, repeat in X months, refer), track follow-up imaging against nodule and lesion guidelines, produce a structured PCP handoff (FHIR), document loop closure and route to a price-transparent cash referral network. Sold as a risk-management service. Consumers can buy a $99 second-opinion review.
why_now: Elective screening boomed in 2025-26 (Function-Ezra, Neko US launch, MCED tests despite NHS-Galleri missing its primary endpoint in May 2026). Medscape and radiology press now describe a 'medical cascade', so reputation and liability risk are becoming visible to operators.
revenue_model: $40-150 per flagged member (B2B), plus annual tracking fee per incidental finding, plus consumer second-opinion upsell.
non_obvious_insight: Screening companies are paid at the scan, but the costs of false positives and lost follow-ups land months later on nobody. Because they are not care providers, they cannot build the follow-up function in-house, so it converts to a compliance product.
first_30_days: Sell a pilot to three regional imaging centers or longevity clinics that resell whole-body MRI. Staff one part-time radiologist and one RN navigator, run follow-up tracking with SMS and a spreadsheet, and charge $75 per flagged patient. Publish a 'follow-up leakage' audit as the sales asset.

title: Magnetic Maps for GPS-Denied Drone Navigation
one_liner: A data company that maps low-altitude magnetic anomalies and sells the layers that let cheap drones navigate without GPS.
customer: Drone makers and integrators in Drone Dominance and Navy autonomy programs who need GPS-denied performance, and later defense agencies seeking quantum navigation.
problem: Jamming defeats GPS, and magnetic navigation needs detailed low-altitude field maps. Public datasets are coarse, and hardware teams do not want to become mapping companies. The Navy is asking for quantum navigation and degraded-environment navigation.
solution: Fly survey drones carrying vector magnetometers over test ranges, training areas and border regions, publish tiles through an API, and provide a reference navigation filter that drone makers can integrate. Start with the Gauntlet region and US test ranges.
why_now: Cheap, sensitive magnetometers and onboard compute make magnetic navigation practical for small drones. Fleets of attritable drones can also continuously enrich the map. The Navy calls for quantum and degraded-network navigation (verify map resolution claims).
revenue_model: Per-area annual licences ($20-100K per region), per-tile API access, and custom survey work for programs. Defense SBIR funding for range expansion.
non_obvious_insight: The map, not the sensor, is the moat and it compounds. Every drone that flies with a magnetometer improves the map, so the mapping firm becomes the network owner.
first_30_days: Buy two survey rigs and map one test range and one agricultural area. Publish accuracy results. Offer 3 Gauntlet participants a pilot navigation filter and tile access.

title: Memory Safe-Harbor: Stop Shredding Server DRAM
one_liner: A component-level sanitization policy plus a resale desk that lets neoclouds and enterprises reuse retired DRAM, CPUs and GPUs instead of shredding whole servers.
customer: Neoclouds, colocation operators, banks and healthcare IT asset managers refreshing servers, with ITADs as the channel. They pay a fixed fee and take a resale share.
problem: Data-center hardware turns over in 12-18 months and a GPU server rack can exceed $1M. DRAM is up about 400% since early 2024. Many enterprise policies still shred whole servers, destroying volatile memory that holds no persistent data. One client reportedly gained 'eight figures' just by pre-triaging refurbish versus scrap.
solution: Publish and audit a per-server-model matrix of which components persist data (SSDs, NVDIMMs, BMC and NIC flash, TPMs) and which do not (DIMMs, most compute and mechanical parts). Get it signed off by a security auditor and the client's CISO. Then run the part-out desk. Data-bearing parts are wiped or destroyed with serialized custody. Everything else is graded, tested and sold to secondary buyers.
why_now: The 2025-26 memory price spike turns shredding into a cash-burning act. AI capex has created huge, fast-cycling retiring fleets, and Sumitomo's GreenTek acquisition shows ITAD is being bought as a trading business.
revenue_model: 40-60% resale share to the client after costs, a $10-30K policy and audit fee per client, and a per-serial chain-of-custody fee.
non_obvious_insight: 'Shred everything' is a compliance habit, not a security requirement. The barrier is organizational sign-off, not technology. Whoever ships a pre-approved risk framework gets inventory that no one else can touch.
first_30_days: Write a 10-page component sanitization matrix for the 5 most common GPU and CPU server models. Have a security-audit firm review it. Pitch 10 neocloud and colo IT asset leads and 5 mid-size ITADs. Run a one-rack pilot on revenue share.
